summary.summary: Target 192.168.92.131 was re-scanned after a prior session that only recorded SSH open. This run found port 80 (Apache/2.4.69 Debian) newly present alongside SSH (22, OpenSSH 9.3p2 Debian, tcpwrapped banner on this scan but previously confirmed as OpenSSH). The web root serves the stock Apache2 Debian default page, which whatweb corroborated (no CMS/app framework fingerprinted). robots.txt discloses a disallowed path, /backup/, which is the textbook robots.txt-leaks-a-hidden-path pattern - but fetching it showed it is only a 16-byte static placeholder page ('old site backup'), not an actual archive or sensitive file. A root-level gobuster run also surfaced /admin/, not referenced in robots.txt, which returns an Apache mod_autoindex directory listing. Critically, when the listing's actual link content was inspected (not just inferred from the directory name), it contained no real file entries - only the standard sort-header links and a parent-directory link. This means /admin is either currently empty or holds only dotfiles hidden by Apache's default IndexIgnore. A targeted ffuf pass with extensions (.php/.txt/.zip/.sql/.bak) against both /admin and /backup using a stack-tailored wordlist found nothing beyond uniform 403s on .htaccess/.htpasswd/.hta-family names - these are Apache's hardcoded protections and fire whether or not the file exists, so they are not evidence of a real file being present. Net effect: this session's main actionable surface is the HTTP service's two discovered-but-currently-inert paths, worth periodic re-checking since the box may populate /admin or /backup with real content later (directory listing being left on is itself a configuration weakness), plus the unchanged SSH service for credential-based entry once credentials are found elsewhere.
summary.attack_surface:
<item>TCP 22 - SSH (OpenSSH 9.3p2 Debian, confirmed in prior session; this run's banner grab was inconclusive but port is open)</item>
<item>TCP 80 - HTTP, Apache/2.4.69 (Debian), serving the stock default page</item>
<item>/robots.txt discloses Disallow: /backup/ (reconnaissance leak, not an access control)</item>
<item>/backup/ - public, returns a static placeholder page, autoindex not triggered (index.html present)</item>
<item>/admin/ - public, Apache directory listing (autoindex) enabled, currently showing no linked files</item>
<item>/.htaccess, /.htpasswd, /.hta - all return 403 server-wide (Apache default protection, not confirmation of file existence)</item>
</attack_surface>
<leads>
<item>Re-check /admin/ and /backup/ periodically - directory listing being enabled on /admin is a real misconfiguration that could expose files if/when content is added or if dotfiles are present but hidden from the index; try explicit guesses (e.g. /admin/.git, /admin/config, known filenames) if context suggests an app that would deploy there</item>
<item>robots.txt as a map of 'things the admin doesn't want crawled' is itself intel - confirm there are no other Disallow entries missed and consider checking for a sitemap.xml too</item>
<item>No CMS/app was fingerprinted on port 80 (plain Debian default page) - if the real application lives on a virtual host, a vhost fuzz against a guessed domain name would be the next web step once a hostname is known (none was discoverable this run - no DNS service, no Host-based hints in headers or page content)</item>
<item>SSH remains the most direct remote-access vector once any credentials are harvested from the web side; keep it in scope for a future credential-stuffing or key-based attack path once leads from HTTP are exhausted</item>
</leads>

timeline.text: Confirmed: whatweb shows a stock Apache Debian default page (no CMS fingerprint), and robots.txt explicitly discloses `/backup/` as disallowed - a classic case of robots.txt leaking a path that's meant to be hidden rather than protected. Let's look directly at `/backup/` and then do a directory enumeration pass.

We found two interesting directories: `/backup/` (content is just a text label "old site backup" - likely a directory listing or placeholder, worth deeper enumeration for actual backup files) and `/admin/` (new, undiscovered via robots.txt, could be a login panel). Let's inspect `/admin/` directly and enumerate inside both directories for actual files (e.g., .zip, .tar, .sql, .php).

We've now got a clear picture. Key insight: the `/admin/` directory returned an Apache autoindex (directory listing) page, but its actual link list only contained the standard sort-column headers and the parent directory link - no real files are listed. That tells us the directory is either genuinely empty right now or contains only dotfiles that Apache's default `IndexIgnore` hides from the listing (and Apache's hardcoded 403 on `.ht*` patterns fires regardless of whether such files actually exist - a classic false-positive trap when fuzzing extensions). `/backup/index.html` is real and returns a 16-byte placeholder page ("old site backup"), not an actual backup archive - the “backup” is cosmetic/content, not a leftover file. This is a good lesson in verifying with `fetch_page` rather than assuming directory names or robots.txt entries mean live artifacts.
